archetype.name: Game Manager (check-down heavy)
archetype.definition: Through four games Jones is a low-aggression distributor working underneath in an offense whose run game is doing the heavy lifting, a sharp retreat from the downfield efficiency he showed in 2025.

report.headline: The 2025 breakout is gone; the run game is carrying a check-down passer.
report.take:
Daniel Jones arrived in Indianapolis last year and had the best season of his career: 8.08 yards per attempt (7th), +0.193 EPA per play (11th), an 8.2-yard aDOT. Four games into 2026, almost none of that has carried over. His -0.171 EPA per dropback ranks 36th of 42, his 5.71 YPA is 37th, and his intended air yards have dropped to 6.02, with throws landing 2.7 yards short of the sticks on average. Those numbers look much more like his 2023 Giants season (5.68 YPA, -0.214 EPA) than his Colts debut. For now he is a game manager, and not an especially clean one.

The protection is not the problem. He has been pressured on just 15.9% of dropbacks, 7th-lowest among 32 charted passers, and his 27.3% pressure-to-sack rate is about where it has sat for most of his career. The damage comes from what he does with clean pockets. A full 25 of his 132 attempts (19%) have gone behind the line of scrimmage, and those plays have produced -0.607 EPA with a 16% success rate. The screen and swing game, Jonathan Taylor at -0.372 EPA per target included, is actively killing drives. The deep ball has vanished as well: 1 of 9 with an interception. Add four interceptions and three lost fumbles, and he has seven giveaways in four games.

The passing game still works in one place. When he throws 10-19 yards (+0.505 EPA, 60% success) or between the numbers (+0.461 EPA, 63% success), the offense moves. In the red zone he is 12 of 16 with three scores. Josh Downs (+0.486 EPA per target) has been the one reliable connection. The Colts are 2-2 and won the last two despite Jones posting -6.9 and -13.4 passing EPA in those games. They did it with the league's most efficient rushing offense (+0.121 EPA per carry, 1st). Week 4 at Washington, 143 yards on 34 attempts with a 2.9% aggressiveness rate, reads like a staff that has started protecting the game from its quarterback.

The outlook depends on whether the receiver room refills and the staff lets him throw intermediate again. Keenan Allen is out this week and Alec Pierce is on IR until late October. That leaves Downs, Tyler Warren and Laquon Treadwell, which explains some of the conservatism. His career CPOE was positive every year from 2022 to 2025, so the -1.76 now is probably partly noise. The fumbles should calm down too. A return to 2025 levels needs more than regression, though: it needs a bigger menu of throws than this offense is currently giving him.

strengths.title: Intermediate and middle-of-field throws
strengths.body: His 10-19 yard throws are producing +0.505 EPA with a 60% success rate, and passes to the middle are at +0.461. This is the profile that drove his 2025 season, and it is the healthiest part of his game now. The sample is small (25 intermediate attempts), but it matches what he did last year, so it should hold if the staff calls more of it.

strengths.title: Red-zone efficiency
strengths.body: Inside the 20 he is 12 of 16 with three touchdowns, no turnovers and +0.595 EPA per play. He has added a designed-run touchdown, and all five of his designed runs have been successes. Sixteen plays is a hint rather than a trend, but the condensed field suits his preference for short, defined reads.

strengths.title: Clean pockets from his line
strengths.body: He is pressured on only 15.9% of dropbacks, 7th-lowest among charted passers, and only 23.9% of his dropbacks face the blitz. His bad-throw rate of 9.1% (11th) says the ball is mostly going where he intends. The bottom-tier efficiency comes from decisions and route depth rather than a collapsing pocket, which is the more fixable problem.

concerns.title: Behind-the-line game is a drain
concerns.body: Nineteen percent of his attempts go behind the line of scrimmage. Those plays average -0.607 EPA with a 16% success rate, and his 6.02 intended air yards with throws 2.7 yards short of the sticks show how much the offense is living there. Part of this is the staff hiding a thin receiver room. It is still a scheme-and-decision choice that caps the whole passing game until it changes.

concerns.title: Seven giveaways in four games
concerns.body: He has four interceptions, one in every game, and three lost fumbles, which ranks 40th of 42. Ball security has been a career-long issue: his INT ranks were in the 30s and 40s most seasons. Losing three of four fumbles is partly bad luck that should even out. The interceptions look more like who he is.

concerns.title: Deep passing has disappeared
concerns.body: He has completed one of nine throws of 20+ air yards, with an interception and a -28 CPOE. Pierce has played only two games and is on IR, and Allen is now out, so the vertical options are thin. It is also a small sample. Even so, the drop from an 8.2 aDOT last year to 6.02 means defenses can squeeze everything underneath.

trend.note: After a strong Week 2 at Kansas City (+5.9 passing EPA, 25.8% aggressiveness), he posted -6.9 against Houston and a season-worst -13.4 at Washington. Week 4 came on a 4.5-yard intended depth with almost no tight-window throws, as the receiver room thinned.

nextGame.headline: Pittsburgh smothers short passes, exactly where Jones now lives
nextGame.body:
Pittsburgh's defense splits sharply by depth. It is stout underneath, allowing -0.094 EPA on short passes (8th), and leaky downfield, at 27th in deep EPA and 30th in explosive pass rate. That is a bad fit for a quarterback who is 1 of 9 deep and throwing 19% of his passes behind the line. The Steelers also generate sacks (8th in sack rate), and Jones turns 27.3% of pressures into sacks. Quarterbacks have managed just 12.3 PPR points per game against them, 3rd-fewest. The opening is on the ground: Pittsburgh ranks 20th against the run, and Indianapolis has the league's most efficient rushing offense.

Availability cuts both ways. Keenan Allen (64% of snaps) is out and Alec Pierce remains on IR, so Jones is down to Josh Downs, Tyler Warren and Laquon Treadwell as primary targets. For Pittsburgh, starting corner Jamel Dean (73% of snaps) is doubtful and could miss a couple of weeks. That further weakens a secondary that already gives up explosives, but it only matters if Indianapolis is willing to throw downfield. Rotational DT Derrick Harmon on IR slightly helps the Colts' run game.

keyMatchups.title: Short passing vs a top-eight short defense
keyMatchups.body: Jones' offense runs through throws under 10 yards, and Pittsburgh is one of the better teams at stopping them. Unless the Colts open up the intermediate game, where Jones has been effective, expect another low-yardage, check-down afternoon.

keyMatchups.title: Colts run game vs PIT front
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis ranks 1st in rushing EPA, and Pittsburgh ranks 20th against the run with a rotational lineman now on IR. A run-heavy script keeps Jones' volume down, but it also keeps him away from the long-yardage downs where he has struggled.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots with Dean out
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh's 27th-ranked deep defense, now likely without Dean, is the one place this matchup is generous. Jones has not hit a deep ball all season, and his top vertical options are hurt, so the opening may go unused.

nextGame.watch: Watch whether Indianapolis takes even two or three shots 15+ yards downfield against a Dean-less secondary, or keeps feeding screens into Pittsburgh's strength.

restOfSeason.body:
Some bounce-back is likely. He has been a positive-CPOE passer four years running, the fumble-loss rate should cool, and Pierce's return around late October would restore a downfield element. The intermediate success suggests the arm and the reads are intact. What has changed is the menu of throws he gets.

The ceiling is lower than 2025, though. With the league's best rushing offense, there is little reason for the staff to put the game in his hands. His rushing has also shrunk from a weapon to a short-yardage tool (21 yards on 11 carries), so he cannot cover for weak passing days with his legs. Expect something close to his Giants-era norm: around 200 passing yards, a touchdown-plus per game, and interceptions that remain a weekly risk.
swingFactors: Pierce's return from IR and Allen's health
Staff willingness to call intermediate and deep throws over screens

bets.reason: The Colts have covered three straight, and their league-best rushing offense meets a Pittsburgh run defense ranked 20th. Pittsburgh's own offense is 25th in EPA and 27th passing, so a field-goal-sized spread looks generous.

Both passing offenses sit near the bottom (Colts 30th, Steelers 27th in pass EPA), and the Colts' last two games went under as they leaned on the run. Pittsburgh's leaky deep defense is the main risk, but Jones hasn't been able to exploit that kind of opening.

bets.lean: At least one, in line with his season
bets.reason: He has thrown an interception in all four games, and his career INT ranks are consistently poor. Pittsburgh's top-eight short-pass defense attacks the area where his offense lives.

Allen is out, Pierce is on IR, and Pittsburgh is strong underneath. The Colts' most efficient path is the run game. Pittsburgh does allow 238 passing yards a game to quarterbacks, which keeps this a lean rather than a strong play.

confidence.note: Four-game sample, but the drop is consistent across games and lines up with a thinned receiver room and a long career baseline.
